post_text:
Contract changes are integrity risks.

I optimized the payload.

As the domain owner, I felt confident simplifying the response for our highest-volume internal API. I thought the contract change was purely an optimization; why send data 95% of consumers ignore? I updated the OpenAPI spec and deployed.

Our service metrics were perfect: low latency, high throughput. Everything was green. 📈

A week later, the BI team flagged a small, persistent discrepancy in cohort data—a few hundred users were missing critical attributes. No alerts fired.

We traced the data lineage back through three services. The root cause was a downstream consumer (Service B) silently failing its internal integrity check because the field I made optional was missing. Service B wrote corrupted records successfully.

The damage was invisible because the failure mode was a successful write of bad data, not an HTTP 500. The cost wasn't CPU cycles; it was weeks of corrupted user profiles. This was the ownership gap 🧩. 💔

The Moral 👇

An API contract is a shared integrity boundary, not merely a data transfer specification.
lesson_extracted: Silent success on a corrupted record is the most dangerous failure mode in distributed systems.
